one_liner: Benchmark repo: hand-scalarised AssemblyScript TinyMT32 beats a TypeScript port 1.25-1.42x on ints and Emscripten C++ slightly.
what_it_does: Implements the 32-bit TinyMT pseudo-random generator four ways (minimal AssemblyScript, AssemblyScript with Array or StaticArray state, C++ compiled by Emscripten with embind, and a TypeScript port) and times them with vitest bench on Node 24.18.0, plus output size. The Wasm modules export seed(u32), int() and float() over module-global state; it is a benchmark and write-up, not a packaged library.
how_it_is_fast: The fast build keeps TinyMT's 128-bit state in four u32 Wasm globals instead of an array, so nextState/temper compile to straight-line i32 ops with no linear-memory loads, bounds checks or runtime library, and the module is 591 bytes. Float output uses a single f32 reinterpret of the bit pattern (reinterpret<f32>) where the TypeScript port allocates an ArrayBuffer, Uint8Array and DataView per call, which is the whole source of the 44-87x float gap.
when_to_use: As a worked example of how to write AssemblyScript that actually beats V8-JIT TypeScript: scalar locals and globals only, no Array, StaticArray or string.
When you need a tiny (about 1.3 KB wasm plus glue) seeded TinyMT32 stream in a browser or Node and are willing to copy the pattern rather than the code (no licence).
When choosing between AssemblyScript and Emscripten for small hot kernels and output size matters: 1,260 bytes vs 36,445 bytes for C++/embind here.
When a TypeScript hot path converts integer bit patterns to floats through ArrayBuffer/DataView allocations; the float rows show what that allocation costs.
when_not_to_use: As a dependency: there is no licence file, no package and five commits, so it is reference material only.

If your AssemblyScript code needs arrays or other stdlib types: the Array and StaticArray builds are 3.7-5.1x slower than TypeScript (2.70-3.23M vs 12.24M hz at 10 ints per call, derived from page data) and 4.6-5x larger.

As proof that Wasm beats JavaScript generally: the integer win is 1.25-1.42x against a TypeScript port that keeps state in a number[] array, and the float win disappears if the TS port reuses one shared typed-array view instead of allocating per call.
When you need multiple independent streams: state lives in module globals, so each generator needs its own Wasm instance.
When native code is an option: the README's native rows are 2.4-3.4x faster than the best Wasm build, though see the gotcha on how they were measured.

integration.dependencies: AssemblyScript compiler (asc ^0.28.20) for the Wasm build; Emscripten for the C++ contender; vitest ^5 for the bench
integration.min_toolchain: AssemblyScript 0.28 (asc), Node 24.18.0 as tested; C++20 for the C++ contender (std::bit_cast)
integration.platforms: any Wasm engine (Node, browsers); the build enables simd, relaxed-simd and stringref features although the generator uses none of them
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: one global state per Wasm instance; not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same seed/int/float shape and same output sequence as the TypeScript port (both pass the reference TinyMT vectors), but AssemblyScript int() returns a signed i32, so callers must apply >>> 0 to get the unsigned value

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the native rows: src/cpp/main.cpp declares a local 'uint32_t seed = 44983921329;' that shadows the seed() function and never calls it, so the global TinyMT inst stays all-zero; that is a fixed point of next_state, so every native u32() returns 0 and f32() returns 0.0f. The README's 'native C++ is 2-4x faster than Wasm' rows therefore time a degenerate generator (temper branch always untaken), not the seeded workload the Wasm and TypeScript rows run. The native build also uses -O3 -Oz, so -Oz applies.

Exported int() is typed i32, so roughly half of the outputs come back negative in JavaScript; the repo's own Wasm test needs int() >>> 0 to match the reference values, while the TypeScript and C++/embind versions return unsigned numbers.

Uneven contenders: the C++ build is size-optimised (em++ -O3 -Oz, last flag wins) and every call crosses an embind JS invoker plus an indirect call, while AssemblyScript exports are called directly; the TypeScript port stores its state in a number[] array while the winning AssemblyScript build uses four scalar globals (the array-based AssemblyScript builds lose to TypeScript 3.7-5.1x). The bench callbacks also discard return values, leaving V8 free to drop the TypeScript tempering step (not checked).

The README's native x10,000 table prints 19,315.69 hz for AssemblyScript, which is the C++/Emscripten figure (AssemblyScript measured 21,602.44), and the committed C++ artifacts (tinymt.wasm 12,350 bytes, tinymt.js 25,519 bytes) do not match the size table (12,143 and 24,302).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over xoroshiro128starstar (an AssemblyScript PRNG measured at about 1.10x Math.random) or superfasthash (about 1.21x over its JS twin) only as a teaching reference for what AssemblyScript style wins and loses, since it measures one algorithm across AssemblyScript, Emscripten C++ and TypeScript side by side; for a usable seeded PRNG package take a licensed sibling.
verified_claims_summary: First-party vitest bench on Node 24.18.0 (CPU and OS not stated): minimal AssemblyScript 15.30M calls/s vs C++/Emscripten 14.22M vs TypeScript 12.24M at 10 ints per call (1.25x over TypeScript), 21,602 vs 19,316 vs 15,175 hz at 10,000 ints (1.42x); floats at 10,000 per call 20,544 vs 17,688 vs 234.66 hz, an 87x gap caused by the TypeScript port allocating an ArrayBuffer, Uint8Array and DataView per float. Native rows (clang++ -O3 -Oz with nanobench) come from an unseeded all-zero generator and are not comparable.
status_note: Five commits on 2026-09-21/22, 0 stars, no licence and no issues; reference only, useful as a write-up rather than as code to vendor.
